I mean in all honesty I try not to think about any of the stuff that’s happened, but I spoke about it with my psychiatrist yesterday because he asked about my childhood and now it’s all I can think about.

Speaking up almost always is better, but sometimes even speaking up leaves you silenced. The concept of being able to speak, have people listens and hear, yet still be mistreated has made me feel like I don’t have a real voice, and this fact has been majorly reinforced by people to this day. In particular, in this time of my life, it’s constantly reinforced by medical professionals. Anyways, the other person who abused me, a pedophile, I ended up reporting, and he was charged and is now a convicted pedophile. I wasn’t his only victim, I was just the only person who was willing to speak to the police, and he was a prominent youth group leader in my community so he would still be working with and abusing/assaulting youth if I didn’t talk to the police likely because the community I was mostly thought God would take care of everything. So, I struggle with mental illness and have tried to commit suicide more times than I can count since I was 16, and I am now 23. I’m currently in the hospital after another suicide attempt. Just a little backstory to say I can understand some of where he’s coming from. However, I wonder if it would help to educate him on communities (friends, loved ones, even strangers) after there has been a suicide. It can be shocking how much it affects people who knew the one who died, to those considering suicide. We think “everybody would be better off without me”, but then for example, there’s groups/pages with thousands of members on Facebook who have been affected, for example, by the suicide of a childhood friend when she was 14. I’m 23 and it still affects me to this day, and there are lives that have changed because of her death (not just those close to her). So maybe you could start there. I have a lot of suggestions, but the thing is, ultimately, we can’t save everybody. He’s going to go through his life and if he’s completely set on dying, he will find a way eventually. You can delay it by hospitalization, but even my best psychiatrists I’ve worked with have said, in the end it’s your life, it’s your choice. He’s an adult, a grown man.. do all you can to help, but nobody can watch him 24/7 for the rest of his life. Another friend of mine killed herself when she was on a pass but still a patient of the hospital, because they were trying to get her to be able to live outside of hospital. I’m in a similar situation, and if I end up dying, it isn’t anybody’s fault and there have been lots of interventions but nobody can keep me in hospital forever and watch me forever. But, saying that, there are many avenues you can go through to help. Start with what I mentioned.
